Overview

Designing a communication system for defence convoys — from nothing.

The Convoy Management System is a full-stack HMI application designed for Indian defence vehicles. It handles real-time navigation, vehicle-to-vehicle communication, emergency alerting, satellite configuration, and system diagnostics — all from a fixed in-cabin display mounted in the lead vehicle.

There was no prior system. No legacy screens to reference, no incumbent product to redesign. The brief was to design a communications platform that worked in the field, under operational conditions, for operators who don't have the luxury of thinking twice.

The core constraint: every screen has to work on the first tap. Operators are moving vehicles. They may be under stress. They're wearing gloves. They have one hand. The interface cannot afford cognitive load — it has to offload it.

I led UX design across the full product with a team of one other designer, working directly with engineering and the product owner at Avantel, a defence communication systems company based in Hyderabad.

The design challenge
01

Information density vs clarity

The home screen needs to show live navigation, convoy unit status, indent information, speed, distance, ETA, barrier warnings, and quick contacts — simultaneously. The challenge was deciding what lives at surface level and what gets one tap away. Hierarchy, not hiding.

02

Designing for high-stress environments

A convoy operator under pressure cannot be presented with menus. The SOS screen — 7 alert categories, one tap each — was the clearest expression of this constraint. Large tap targets. Icon-led. No confirmation dialogs for time-critical actions. Every decision had to ask: what does this look like when things go wrong?

03

A system beneath the interface

CMS sits on top of satellite communication hardware — TDMA frequencies, TxRx configuration, satellite beam data, LDPC encoding. The settings screens had to make complex RF parameters manageable for field technicians who know the domain but shouldn't need a manual. Technical density without visual chaos.

The product

Rather than a process walkthrough, what follows is the actual product — annotated with the decisions that shaped each screen. This is what shipped to Avantel's engineering team.

01 — Navigation module
Home — Live Navigation + Indent Info
The home screen is a split layout: the map fills the left ~65%, the indent information panel takes the right. Three persistent data points ride on top of the map — speed (with a visual speedometer arc for glanceable reading), distance, and barrier status. The left sidebar nav stays fixed across all screens so the operator always knows where they are.
Map expanded + Create Barrier
Map expands to full screen. The barrier creation button surfaces from the bottom — contextual, not always visible. Keeps the map uncluttered during normal navigation.
Barrier active — Landslide state
Once a barrier is created the status chip updates from "No Barriers" to the alert type — here, Landslide. Create and Clear actions appear together. State is always surfaced at the top of the map.
02 — SOS module
SOS — Emergency Alert Grid
7 alert categories in a 4+3 grid: Breakdown, Attack, Construction, Lane Closure, Medical, Land Slide, Custom. Large circular tap targets. Icon-first, label below. No confirmation dialog — a single tap sends the alert instantly. This was the most deliberate decision in the product: in an emergency, confirmation is a liability.
03 — Messaging module
Messages — Inbox view
Tabbed inbox / outbox / sent. Message log shows ID, sender, recipient, type, timestamp. Row-level actions for view and delete. Compose lives top-right — always one tap from any tab.
Compose — Text + Predefined phrases
The big decision here: predefined tactical phrases (Stop Immediately, Enemies Ahead, Medical Emergency, Maintain Formation, GPS Signal Lost) as tappable chips. For field comms, a pre-composed message is faster and more reliable than free text. Voice messaging is one tab away.
Compose — Voice Message with waveform playback
Voice messages display as waveform strips with duration. Multiple recordings can be staged before sending. The microphone button floats bottom-right — always accessible, consistent across compose modes. Text, voice, and predefined phrases all live under one compose flow with tab switching — one mental model, three input modes.
04 — Calls module
Calls — Contact list + Information Transmitted
Split layout: contact list left, transmission history right. Each contact shows vehicle type and model. Three actions per row — call, message, favourite — without going anywhere. The right panel shows a live log of what's been transmitted to the selected contact.
Calls — Dial Pad + Recent Logs
Classic dialpad on the left, recent contacts on the right. The Call button spans the full width of the dialpad column — large, unambiguous, hard to miss. Contact List, Call History, and Dial Pad are tab-switchable beneath.
05 — Settings & administration
Settings — Category overview
Grouped into Manage, Device & Hardware, Communication, System. Slide-over panel keeps the operator contextually on the home screen.
Satellite Beam Configuration
Data Tx, Rx, Signalling, and TDMA frequencies in a scannable table. Set to HW pushes config to hardware.
Build In Test (BIT) — Module status
Baseband, GPS, Modem, SSPA, Rx Front End — each with a PASS/FAIL badge and last-checked timestamp. "Perform BIT" triggers a fresh diagnostic sweep.
Audio Settings — Output, MIC, Preferences
Grouped into Output, MIC, Audio Preference, and Advanced. Toggle-led. Speaker, internal/external mic, PMC control, sidetone, headset — all surfaced without nesting.
Vehicle Management — Fleet roster
Full fleet registry: ID, type (Jeep 4x4, Bullet Bike, Ambassador, Tata 2515), company, model number, BA number. Edit and delete per row. Add Vehicle floats top-right.
Key design decisions
Decision 01 — SOS
"Should emergency alerts require confirmation?"

We chose no confirmation dialog for SOS. In a genuine emergency — attack, medical crisis, breakdown — a second tap costs time the operator may not have. The large circular icons with clear labels (not just icons alone) reduce mis-taps enough that the risk of false alerts was lower than the risk of delayed ones. The interface has to trust the operator.

Decision 02 — Messaging
"How much should the interface assume about what operators need to say?"

Quite a lot. Predefined tactical phrases (Stop Immediately, Enemies Ahead, Maintain Formation) exist because field communication is time-critical and standardised. Free text is there for edge cases, but the default experience leads with chips. Reducing the message composition task to a single tap is not laziness — it's operational design.

Decision 03 — Navigation
"How much map do operators actually need?"

The default home screen gives the map ~65% of the content area, with the indent info panel taking the rest. An expand control lets operators go full-screen map when needed. We resisted the temptation to add more data overlays to the map — the three persistent status chips (speed, distance, barriers) are enough at a glance. More information is not more useful in a moving vehicle.

Decision 04 — Settings
"How do you design for satellite frequencies without making it feel like engineering software?"

Grouping was the answer. Settings are organised by function (Manage, Device & Hardware, Communication, System), not by technical category. Satellite beam config shows only what's needed to identify and edit a beam — beam name, lat/long, and the five frequency values. The operator shouldn't need to understand TDMA to configure it.

What I learned
01
Greenfield is not freedom — it's a different kind of constraint

Starting from zero sounds like an opportunity. In practice it means you have no user behaviour to analyse, no legacy patterns to extend, and no existing mental models to map against. You have to build the first version of something and accept that you're getting some of it wrong.

02
The settings section is where UX earns its place in technical products

Anyone can design a clean home screen. The real test is whether you can make satellite beam frequency configuration — with parameters like TDMA TX Freq, LDPC encoding, BPSK modulation — feel navigable. That required grouping, progressive disclosure, and a lot of restraint about what goes on one screen.

03
Designing without user research changes how you evaluate decisions

There was no access to operators for research. Every decision had to be justified through domain reasoning, stakeholder input, and analogous precedents from aviation, maritime, and emergency HMI. You learn to be explicit about your assumptions so engineers can challenge them — and some of them did.

04
Minimal is earned, not assumed

Stripping information from a screen sounds like the safe choice. It isn't. Every time something was removed, the question was: where does the operator go when they need this? Minimalism in operational HMI means every surface carries exactly what's needed — not less, not more. Getting that right takes iteration.
